yamnaya-culture.name: Yamnaya culture
yamnaya-culture.summary: A Copper to early Bronze Age culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (3300–2600 BC), known for pit-grave burials under kurgans and often linked to Proto-Indo-European origins.

david-w-anthony.name: David W. Anthony
david-w-anthony.summary: American anthropologist specializing in horse domestication and Indo-European migrations, known for his book The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

catacomb-culture.name: Catacomb culture
catacomb-culture.summary: A Bronze Age culture of the Pontic steppe, about 2500 to 1950 BCE, descended from the Yamnaya, likely Indo-European-speaking and later succeeded by the Srubnaya culture.

abashevo-culture.name: Abashevo culture
abashevo-culture.summary: A late Middle Bronze Age culture, c. 2200-1850 BC, of the middle Volga and southern Urals, known for metalworking and early chariot use and likely pre-Indo-Iranian speaking.

ukrainian-grey.name: Ukrainian Grey
ukrainian-grey.summary: An ancient, hardy breed of Podolian cattle from Ukraine, traditionally raised for both meat and draught power.

sintashta-culture.name: Sintashta culture
sintashta-culture.summary: A Middle Bronze Age archaeological culture of the Southern Urals (c. 2200–1900 BCE), thought to be the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages and the earliest known chariots, with fortified, militaristic settlements.

srubnaya-culture.name: Srubnaya culture
srubnaya-culture.summary: An Iranic Late Bronze Age culture (1900–1200 BCE) in the eastern Pontic-Caspian steppe, successor to the Yamnaya culture and generally linked to early Iranian speakers.

fatyanovo-balanovo-culture.name: Fatyanovo–Balanovo culture
fatyanovo-balanovo-culture.summary: A Chalcolithic and early Bronze Age culture of the Corded Ware complex that flourished in Russia's forests from about 2900 to 2050 BC, spreading east and mining copper in the Urals.

cucuteni-trypillia-culture.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
cucuteni-trypillia-culture.summary: A Neolithic–Chalcolithic farming culture, about 5050 to 2950 BC, in southeast Europe whose 'mega-site' settlements, some with thousands of structures, were among the largest in the world at the time.

kurgan-stelae.name: Kurgan stelae
kurgan-stelae.summary: Anthropomorphic stone slabs set atop or around kurgan burial mounds, made over more than three millennia by cultures including the Pit Grave culture, the Scythians and Turkic peoples.

scythians.name: Scythians
scythians.summary: An ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people who migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe in the 9th-8th centuries BC, dominating the region through mounted warfare before being conquered by the Sarmatians in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC.

corded-ware-culture.name: Corded Ware culture
corded-ware-culture.summary: A broad European archaeological culture from about 2900 to 2300 BC, likely descended from Yamnaya migrants and a probable vector for spreading Indo-European languages.

globular-amphora-culture.name: Globular Amphora culture
globular-amphora-culture.summary: A Central European archaeological culture from about 3400 to 2800 BC, named for its globular pottery and preceding the Corded Ware culture.

arkaim.name: Arkaim
arkaim.summary: A fortified archaeological site (c. 2150–1650 BC) of the Sintashta culture in Russia's Southern Urals, discovered in 1987 and linked to early Proto-Indo-Iranian speakers.

vedas.name: Vedas
vedas.summary: A large body of ancient Indian religious texts and the oldest layer of Sanskrit literature, orally transmitted since the 2nd millennium BCE and regarded as the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.

avesta.name: Avesta
avesta.summary: The corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally over centuries before being written down under the Sasanians and later largely lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran.

kemi-oba-culture.name: Kemi Oba culture
kemi-oba-culture.summary: An archaeological culture (c. 3700–2200 BC) near the Sea of Azov and the lower Bug, Dnieper and Crimea, overlapping with the Catacomb culture.

yama.name: Yama
yama.summary: Hindu god of death and justice who judges the souls of the dead; Vedic tradition holds he was the first mortal to die and find the way to the afterlife.

rigveda.name: Rigveda
rigveda.summary: An ancient collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, the oldest known Vedic text and one of the four sacred Hindu Vedas, most likely composed between about 1500 and 1000 BCE in northwestern India.

menhir.name: Menhir
menhir.summary: A large upright stone placed by humans, typically from the Bronze Age, found across Europe, Africa and Asia and thought to have served ritual or territorial purposes.

southern-ural.name: Southern Ural
southern-ural.summary: The wide southern stretch of the Ural Mountains, running from the Ufa River to the Ural River between the East European and West Siberian plains.

sintashta.name: Sintashta
sintashta.summary: A fortified Bronze Age settlement (c. 2100–1800 BC) in Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia, known as a metallurgical center and for some of the oldest known chariot burials.

chelyabinsk-oblast.name: Chelyabinsk Oblast
chelyabinsk-oblast.summary: A federal subject of Russia in the Ural Mountains, straddling the border of Europe and Asia, with its administrative center in the city of Chelyabinsk.

poltavka-culture.name: Poltavka culture
poltavka-culture.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological culture that flourished on the Volga-Ural steppe from about 2800 to 2100 BCE, emerging from the Yamnaya culture and considered ancestral to Indo-Iranian peoples.

krivoye-lake.name: Krivoye Lake
krivoye-lake.summary: Small oxbow lake in Russia's Chelyabinsk Oblast, best known for a chariot burial found there dated to around 2000 BC, among the earliest known.

andronovo-culture.name: Andronovo culture
andronovo-culture.summary: A group of related Late Bronze Age cultures from about 2000 to 1150 BCE, spanning from the southern Urals to central Siberia and western Xinjiang, generally agreed to have been Indo-Iranian.

mitanni.name: Mitanni
mitanni.summary: A Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia, around 1550 to 1260 BCE, a major regional power bordered by the Hittites, Egyptians, Kassites and Assyrians.

proto-indo-european-language.name: Proto-Indo-European language
proto-indo-european-language.summary: The reconstructed common ancestor of all Indo-European languages, likely spoken from about 4500 to 2500 BCE, possibly originating in the Pontic-Caspian steppe.

pontic-caspian-steppe.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
pontic-caspian-steppe.summary: A vast grassland stretching from the northern Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, corresponding to ancient Scythia and Sarmatia, and thought to be where horses were first domesticated.

kamyana-mohyla.name: Kamyana Mohyla
kamyana-mohyla.summary: An archaeological site in Ukraine with petroglyphs ranging from the Upper Paleolithic to medieval times, found inside sandstone caves and grottoes.

proto-indo-europeans.name: Proto-Indo-Europeans
proto-indo-europeans.summary: A prehistoric Eurasian people, likely living in the Pontic-Caspian steppe between about 6400 and 3500 BC, whose descendants spread across Eurasia including the Hittites and Mycenaean Greeks.

trito.name: *Trito
trito.summary: Figure in reconstructed Proto-Indo-European mythology, regarded as the first warrior and a culture hero. He defeats a three-headed serpent and keeps up the cycle of giving between gods and mortals.

seima-turbino-culture.name: Seima-Turbino culture
seima-turbino-culture.summary: A pattern of Bronze Age burial sites across northern Eurasia sharing similar bronze artifacts, linked to nomadic warrior-metalworkers who traveled on horseback or two-wheeled carts, dated to about 2200 to 1900 BCE.

indo-iranian-languages.name: Indo-Iranian languages
indo-iranian-languages.summary: The largest branch of the Indo-European language family, with over 300 languages spoken by about 1.7 billion people across South Asia, West Asia and Central Asia.

lola-culture.name: Lola culture
lola-culture.summary: A Middle Bronze Age culture that flourished in the North Caucasus and Volga-Ural steppes from about 2200 to 1800 BC.

north-caucasus.name: North Caucasus
north-caucasus.summary: Subregion of Eastern Europe, part of Russia, forming the northern part of the Caucasus between the Black and Caspian seas and the Caucasus Mountains; came under Russian control in the 19th century.

volosovo-culture.name: Volosovo culture
volosovo-culture.summary: An archaeological culture of forest foragers around the middle Volga and Kama basin, emerging between the 4th and 3rd millennium BC and lasting into the 2nd millennium BC.

country-of-towns.name: Land of Towns
country-of-towns.summary: A term for a cluster of more than twenty fortified Bronze Age settlements, around 2,000 BC, discovered in the southern Trans-Urals; Arkaim is the best known site.

proto-indo-iranian-religion.name: Proto-Indo-Iranian religion
proto-indo-iranian-religion.summary: The reconstructed religion of the early Indo-Iranian peoples, including concepts like universal order (rta/asha) and the sacred drink soma/haoma, ancestral to later Iranian and Indo-Aryan religions.

ta.name: Ṛta
ta.summary: In Vedic religion, the principle of cosmic order governing the proper functioning of nature, morality and ritual, later overshadowed by the concepts of dharma and karma.

asha.name: Asha
asha.summary: A Zoroastrian concept meaning truth, righteousness and cosmic order, central to Zoroastrian theology and personified as the divinity Asha Vahishta.

soma-drink.name: Soma
soma-drink.summary: A ritual drink of the early Vedic Indo-Aryan religion, mentioned in the Rigveda and linked to immortality; the plant used to make it is now unknown and debated.

haoma.name: Haoma
haoma.summary: A divine plant in Zoroastrianism and later Persian mythology, rooted in ancient Indo-Iranian religion and the counterpart of the Vedic drink soma.

jamshid.name: Jamshid
jamshid.summary: A mythical king of ancient Iran, called Yima in Zoroastrian scripture, remembered in Persian tradition as the fourth and greatest ruler of the legendary Pishdadian dynasty.

slavic-native-faith.name: Slavic Native Faith
slavic-native-faith.summary: A modern polytheistic religious movement, also called Rodnovery, reviving historical Slavic belief systems alongside other influences such as Hinduism.

roerichism.name: Roerichism
roerichism.summary: Spiritual and cultural movement centred on the Agni Yoga teachings of Helena and Nicholas Roerich, which helped bring knowledge of Asian religions to the Western world.

historical-vedic-religion.name: Historical Vedic religion
historical-vedic-religion.summary: The religious ideas and practices of Indo-Aryan peoples in northwest India during the Vedic period (c. 1500–500 BCE), recorded in Vedic texts and one of the major traditions that shaped modern Hinduism.

steppe-theory.name: Steppe theory (Kurgan hypothesis)
steppe-theory.summary: The leading proposal that the Proto-Indo-European homeland lay among Pontic steppe peoples buried under kurgan burial mounds, who then expanded across Europe and parts of Asia.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.summary: The chief god and sky deity of Zoroastrianism, first prominently invoked in the Achaemenid-era Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great.

varuna.name: Varuna
varuna.summary: A Hindu god originally seen as the sovereign ruler of the sky and cosmic moral order in Vedic times, later transformed into the lord of the waters and oceans.

asura.name: Asura
asura.summary: A class of power-seeking beings in Hindu and Buddhist mythology, related to the more benevolent Deva gods and often described as demigods locked in rivalry with them.

zoroaster.name: Zoroaster
zoroaster.summary: Iranian religious reformer traditionally dated to the 7th-6th centuries BC (some scholars place him earlier), who became the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism through his hymns, the Gathas.

asgard.name: Asgard
asgard.summary: In Norse mythology, the fortified home of the Aesir gods described in the Eddas and other Old Norse texts, roughly equivalent to Mount Olympus in Greek myth.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

deva-hinduism.name: deva
deva-hinduism.summary: A Sanskrit term for 'god' or 'divine being' used for deities in Hinduism, later contrasted in texts with the malevolent Asuras.

daeva.name: Daeva
daeva.summary: In Zoroastrianism, a supernatural being with negative traits, originally described as 'gods to be rejected' in the earliest texts and later seen as promoters of chaos and evil.

indra.name: Indra
indra.summary: The Vedic god of weather, storms and war, regarded as king of the gods in early Hinduism and the most frequently mentioned deity in the Rigveda, celebrated for slaying the demon Vritra.

ahriman.name: Angra Mainyu
ahriman.summary: The destructive evil spirit of Zoroastrianism, the main adversary of the supreme god Ahura Mazda.

southern-bug.name: Southern Bug
southern-bug.summary: A navigable river in Ukraine, 806 kilometres long, that once served as a border between imperial Russia and the Ottomans.

dniester.name: Dniester
dniester.summary: A river in Eastern Europe that flows through Ukraine and Moldova before reaching the Black Sea.

ural-river.name: Ural River
ural-river.summary: A 2,428-kilometre river flowing through Russia and Kazakhstan into the Caspian Sea, conventionally marking part of the boundary between Europe and Asia.

domestication-of-the-horse.name: DOM2
domestication-of-the-horse.summary: Genetic profile linked to the domestication of the horse, with genomic evidence pointing to an origin around 2200 BCE in the Volga-Don region of the Pontic-Caspian steppe.
